tier_reason: The README gives the 4x RapidJSON / 25x nlohmann claims, and its GCC 10 -O3 chart (doc/rome.png) plots simdjson against yyjson, RapidJSON and JSON for Modern C++, with the code in simdjson/benchmark/ (e.g. partial_tweets/rapidjson.h). The linked peer-reviewed VLDB Journal 2019 paper (arXiv 1902.08318) names the CPU as an Intel i7-6700 and the build as GCC 9.1 -O3 -march=native, and its public artifact repo (simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019, experiments/comparison) supplies the code, so code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated.

corrections.workload: README chart (doc/rome.png): single-core throughput in GB/s on load-and-process tasks (partial tweets, kostya, distinct user id, top tweet) against yyjson, RapidJSON and JSON for Modern C++ (code in benchmark/). VLDB Journal 2019 paper, Table 10: full-validating parse of 14 real-world files (twitter.json, canada, citm_catalog, gsoc-2018, ...) against RapidJSON, sajson, nlohmann and others. The README's synthetic file-size scaling chart (doc/growing.png, up to ~3.5 MB) plots simdjson alone, with no baseline.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: "parse JSON 4x faster than RapidJSON and 25x faster than JSON for Modern C++" and "uses three-quarters less instructions than state-of-the-art parser RapidJSON". NDJSON: "3.5 GB/s" (feature bullet) and "we can exceed 3 GB/s" with multithreaded parse_many. Paper Table 10 (Skylake i7-6700), twitter.json: simdjson 2.2 GB/s vs RapidJSON 0.45 GB/s (~4.9x, derived from page data), vs RapidJSON insitu 0.72 GB/s (~3.1x, derived from page data), vs JSON for Modern C++ 0.10 GB/s (~22x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README chart: GNU GCC 10 with -O3; file-size chart: GNU GCC 9 with -O3. VLDB 2019 paper: GNU GCC 9.1 with -O3 -march=native.
corrections.hardware: README: 'Intel Skylake processor (3.4 GHz)', model not named. VLDB 2019 paper: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz base / 3.7 GHz turbo, DDR4-2133) and Intel i3-8121U (Cannon Lake, 2.2 GHz).
corrections.caveats: The legend of the README chart (doc/rome.png) names RapidJSON and 'JSON for M. C++' (nlohmann) along with yyjson, so both headline baselines are in the plotted comparison. Exact bar values are not printed; read visually, they put simdjson at about 2.2-3.2 GB/s against RapidJSON at about 0.4-0.5 GB/s. The README's CPU is given only as 'Skylake 3.4 GHz'; the exact model (i7-6700) comes from the VLDB 2019 paper, whose runs used GCC 9.1 rather than the README chart's GCC 10. The file-size scaling chart has no baseline. The reproducible-experiments repo simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019 is public but archived. GitHub reports Apache-2.0, but the README says the code is also available under MIT (LICENSE-MIT) at the user's choice.

notes: The headline and README numbers check out. The paper's Table 10 backs up the ~4x RapidJSON claim (twitter.json 2.2 vs 0.45 GB/s). Metadata checks out: 24,272 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, not a fork, not archived. The license is dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT, and benchmark_url was kept as the README.

tier_reason: The README Performance tables compare yyjson with rapidjson (insitu and utf8), simdjson and cjson on twitter.json. They state the compiler (gcc 9.3, clang 12) and the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7R32, Apple A14). The public benchmark code in github.com/ibireme/yyjson_benchmark (src/, CMakeLists.txt) fixes the flags: the Release build type by default, plus -march=native.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On AWS EC2 (AMD EPYC 7R32, gcc 9.3), twitter.json: yyjson(insitu) 1.80 GB/s parse / 1.51 GB/s stringify vs rapidjson(insitu) 0.77 GB/s parse (~2.3x, derived from page data), vs rapidjson(utf8) 0.26 GB/s parse / 0.39 GB/s stringify (~6.9x / ~3.9x, derived from page data), vs simdjson 1.52 GB/s parse / 0.61 GB/s stringify (~1.18x / ~2.5x, derived from page data), vs cjson 0.32 GB/s parse / 0.17 GB/s stringify (~5.6x / ~8.9x, derived from page data). On Apple A14 (clang 12): yyjson 2.39 GB/s (3.51 insitu) parse vs simdjson 2.19, rapidjson 0.30 (utf8) / 0.75 (insitu), cjson 0.48.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3 for the EC2 table; clang 12 for the Apple A14 table. yyjson_benchmark's CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release (CMake's default Release flags for GCC/Clang are -O3 -DNDEBUG) and adds -march=native when the compiler supports it. The linked interactive reports also cover msvc 2019 and clang 10.

notes: Every figure in the record matches the README; the only fix was adding the required 'derived from page data' markers to the ratios. Flags are pinned in the public harness CMakeLists (Release + -march=native), so tier A stands. The harness repo was last pushed 2023-06. Metadata checks out: 3,883 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-09-08.

tier_reason: The json_performance README ('Latest results (June 8, 2025)') lists Glaze against RapidJSON, nlohmann, simdjson On-Demand, yyjson and others, with the code public in src/main.cpp. It gives Clang 17 on a MacBook Pro M1, but neither the README nor CMakeLists.txt sets optimization flags or a default build type, so flags are missing and the tier stops at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Glaze 1.01 s roundtrip / 1396 MB/s write / 1200 MB/s read vs RapidJSON 3.76 s / 289 MB/s / 416 MB/s (~3.7x roundtrip, ~4.8x write, ~2.9x read, derived from page data); vs nlohmann 15.44 s / 86 MB/s / 81 MB/s (~15x roundtrip, derived from page data); read 1200 MB/s vs simdjson On-Demand 1163 MB/s (~1.03x, derived from page data); ABC out-of-order-keys test: Glaze reads at 1219 MB/s vs simdjson On-Demand at 89 MB/s (~13.7x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark: the Glaze author runs and publishes it in the companion repo json_performance, using a test object and workload he designed. Results are dated June 8, 2025, which is also the harness repo's last commit. The page states the compiler (Clang 17) and machine (MacBook Pro M1, single core), but the harness's CMakeLists.txt sets only -Wall -Wextra, with no optimization flags and no default build type, so flags are unknown. The simdjson comparison uses a known weak case for simdjson's On-Demand API (out-of-order keys), which the same non-neutral author highlights.

notes: All numbers match the json_performance README and the Glaze README Performance table. Ratios are now marked as derived. Tier C confirmed. Metadata checks out: 3,029 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-09-24, not a fork.

The table has no std::hash row; the nearest stdlib-style entry is FNV64 at 1.2 GB/s. The Murmur3 row is the 32-bit variant, so it is not width-matched against XXH3's 64-bit output. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION because the repo mixes licenses: the library is BSD-2-Clause and the xxhsum CLI is GPLv2-or-later.
